newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Lebed ousting hits Russian securities.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lebed ousting hits Russian securities.

text.p: Russian debt slid on Thursday after President Boris Yeltsin sacked security advisor Alexander Lebed but investors said any short term uncertainty would give way to optimism over the way Yeltsin's firm hand has reinforced the reformist camp.
"Yeltsin's action lanced the boil," said Robin Hubbard, senior emerging market economist at Chase Manhattan in London.
In a television address, Yeltsin said that he could no longer tolerate Lebed's lack of team spirit and naked political amibition.
Immediately after the announcement, dollar-denominated Vneshekonombank debt, foreign commercial loans to the former Soviet Union, was quoted around 74 1/2 percent of face value.
But by 1500 GMT it had recovered to 75 1/2 percent, still down from mid-morning highs of around 76 but still above the day's opening low of 74.
Chase's Hubbard said the long-term impact of the sacking was unclear, but he did not expect debt to trade up to its high of 80 percent of face value, reached earlier this month.

There also was some selling of American Depositary Receipts - dollar denominated securities which avoid the hassles of investing directly - of Russian oil giant LUKoil, but traders said that as the market was short of stock, buyers had soon mopped up any excess.

"I do not know what Lebed will do now," said a Russian equity trader at a major European bank in London, "But this does show that Yeltsin is backing Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and reformer Anatoly Chubais, which is good for the market."
Some investors believe that if Lebed had not been pushed, he would have been forced to go.

"Lebed was the hostage of Yeltsin, not the other way round and Lebed was very short on options. He had the choice to get out or stay in and become compromised," said Mark Cooke a fund manager at Brunswick Capital Management in London.
The sacking comes after increasing public Kremlin infighting, with Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accusing Lebed of plotting a gradual coup while President Boris Yeltsin awaits heart surgery.
One debt trader said there was a danger Lebed could now "dish the dirt", and the market may be in for an unsteady period just as Russia faces key economic tests of sentiment.

The country is on the verge of a Eurobond issue of up to $500 million and RAO Gazprom, the world's largest natural gas producer, is looking for $460 million via the issue of shares which will be listed in London.

"All of these things seem to march forward quite nicely, interest rates are down and the country won a good rating from Standard & Poors," said Daiwa Institute of Research chief political analyst Susanne Schmidt.
In October, S&P assigned Russia a BB-minus long-term foreign currency debt rating, better than that for Brazil or Turkey.
It also said that "short periods of policy stress would not affect Russia's ability to service its debt", a fact which has reassured investors.

"Can you see them all still at each other's throats in four years time? Despite all the shennanigans in the Kremlin, people take a view that this is a big country and it will sort itself out," said Daiwa's Schmidt.
